subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is an immune‑mediated lung disease where Aspergillus colonises the airways of asthmatic or atopic patients, causing bronchial inflammation, mucus plugging and central bronchiectasis.

sections.p: ABPA results from a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus spores that colonise the bronchi of susceptible individuals, most often those with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
b: Type I (IgE) and Type III (immune‑complex) hypersensitivity dominate.
Leads to bronchial inflammation, mucus plugging, and central bronchiectasis.

sections.p: Aspergillus fumigatus is a ubiquitous saprophytic mold producing airborne conidia that are small enough to reach the lower airways.
b: Produces proteases and toxins that aid colonisation but are not directly invasive in ABPA.

sections.p: Spores are inhaled from the environment; they germinate in the bronchial lumen when host immunity is skewed toward an allergic phenotype.
b: No person‑to‑person spread; exposure is environmental.

sections.p: In ABPA the immune response to colonising Aspergillus causes recurrent asthma exacerbations, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, and progressive central bronchiectasis.
b: Eosinophilia, elevated total IgE, and Aspergillus‑specific IgE/IgG are hallmarks.
If untreated, can progress to irreversible airway damage and respiratory failure.

sections.p: Diagnosis combines clinical, radiologic and immunologic criteria (Rosenberg–Patterson).
b: Asthma or cystic fibrosis plus immediate cutaneous reactivity to Aspergillus.
Total IgE >1000 IU/mL, Aspergillus‑specific IgE/IgG, eosinophilia >500/µL.
Chest CT shows central bronchiectasis and fleeting infiltrates.

t.b: Is there a massive IgE response? >1000 IU/mL supports ABPA; lower values make diagnosis less likely.
Confirms sensitisation; high specific IgE/IgG together with clinical picture strengthens diagnosis.
Shows central bronchiectasis and transient infiltrates; if CT unavailable, high‑resolution chest X‑ray may reveal bronchial wall thickening.
Elevated >500/µL supports allergic inflammation; normal count does not exclude ABPA.

sections.p: Management aims to suppress the exaggerated immune response and clear fungal colonisation while preserving lung function.
b: Systemic corticosteroids are first‑line to dampen type I/III hypersensitivity.
Oral antifungal (itraconazole) reduces fungal burden, allowing lower steroid doses.
Bronchodilators and inhaled steroids treat underlying asthma.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams.
b: ABPA occurs in asthmatics with high IgE, eosinophilia, and central bronchiectasis.
Diagnostic criteria: asthma + immediate skin test + elevated IgE + Aspergillus‑specific IgE/IgG + radiologic changes.
Treatment: systemic steroids ± itraconazole; monitor IgE trend to gauge response.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe asthma attack not responding to inhalers
Hemoptysis or massive mucus plugging causing respiratory failure

faq.q: Why does ABPA occur mainly in asthmatics?
faq.a: Asthmatic airways have a Th2‑dominant immune environment that favours IgE‑mediated hypersensitivity to inhaled Aspergillus spores.

faq.q: Can ABPA develop in patients without asthma?
faq.a: Rarely, it can appear in cystic fibrosis; otherwise asthma or another atopic lung disease is required.

faq.q: What distinguishes ABPA from simple Aspergillus colonisation?
faq.a: ABPA shows systemic allergic markers (high IgE, eosinophilia, specific IgE/IgG) and radiologic bronchiectasis, not just a positive culture.

exam: List the Rosenberg–Patterson criteria for diagnosing ABPA.
Explain why systemic corticosteroids are the cornerstone of ABPA therapy and how antifungal agents complement treatment.
Describe the radiologic pattern that differentiates ABPA from other causes of bronchiectasis.
